vignette:
Mona, a 52-year-old married project manager of Middle Eastern background, sought help after months of feeling as if her life had narrowed around a single day. The terror attack itself had taken place during an ordinary commute home, when a bomb went off several streets ahead and sent people running in all directions. In the confusion, Mona had heard the sudden chop of a helicopter overhead and seen police vehicles flooding the intersection, officers shouting for people to move back. The violence was brief but unmistakable: broken glass, screaming, smoke, and the sense that the city had become dangerous in an instant. Since then, the helicopter sound that once blended into the background now made her stomach clench, and the sight of police uniforms or any public display of violence could catch her off guard in a way that felt immediate and bodily. Those moments did not just startle her; they pushed her into a harsh judgment about what had happened to her and what it had done to her identity. She found herself thinking that she used to be a happy person, but now she was always miserable, as if the attack had taken away a part of her that could not be recovered.

In the months that followed, Mona began to feel that she did not know herself anymore. Before the bombing, she had seen herself as composed, efficient, and good at keeping her family and work life steady. Now, when she walked into a building and noticed security or heard a helicopter passing, she felt an abrupt drop inside herself and then the thought that she was no longer the woman she had been. She would look in the mirror and feel detached from the face looking back, as though the frightened expression had become permanent. What disturbed her most was the sense that other people could see what happened to her just by looking at her. She became self-conscious in meetings, convinced colleagues could tell she was damaged, and she would measure her own face for signs of fear before stepping out of the car or greeting a client. The more police presence, violence in the news, or aircraft noise appeared around her, the more those appraisals hardened: each cue seemed to confirm that the attack was not over in any meaningful sense, because it had left visible marks on who she was and how others would read her.

At work, Mona tried to carry on as a project manager, but the environment itself kept placing her near reminders she could not easily avoid. She worked in a downtown office where police cars were a familiar sight outside the building, and once, during a routine emergency drill, the sound of a helicopter passing overhead sent her pulse racing and left her distracted for the rest of the afternoon. After that she started planning routes, timing errands to avoid crowded streets, and declining lunches or after-work gatherings when the topic turned to news footage or public violence. The effort to keep herself together took so much attention that her confidence at work began to fray. She worried not only about being seen as fragile, but about confirming that she was in fact no longer herself. When she noticed a police officer in the lobby or heard rotor blades overhead, she would tense and immediately think of how miserable she had become, as if the cue itself were proof that happiness was something she had lost for good.

Over time, these reactions made the world feel smaller and less familiar. Mona described moving through her days with a constant sense that her true self had been displaced, leaving behind someone watchful, drained, and ashamed. She did not say the attack had ruined everything, but she spoke with a quiet certainty that it had made her visible in the wrong way, as if her distress were written across her face for strangers and coworkers to read. That belief made her withdraw further, and the withdrawal made her feel more estranged from herself. By the time she came to therapy, she was still functioning on the surface, yet she felt trapped in the knowledge that helicopters, police, and violence could bring the whole experience rushing back into her body and into the conviction that she was no longer the happy person she had once been. What finally brought her in was the fear that this sense of being altered and exposed was becoming permanent, and her hope was that she might learn how to feel like herself again without bracing for every siren, uniform, or passing aircraft.
